newsitem.title: USA: ABC deal may show Disney to stay in radio.
newsitem.headline: ABC deal may show Disney to stay in radio.

text.p: The acquisition of radio stations in Detroit and Washington by Walt Disney Co's ABC Radio may demonstrate the company's interest in staying in the radio business, analysts said on Monday.

There had been speculation in some circles that Disney might shed its radio business. The decision to acquire two stations from Evergreen Media Corp and Chancellor Broadcasting Co may indicate Disney has other plans, analysts said.

The passage of the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which increased the number of radio stations that could be owned by companies, might have given Disney more of an incentive to remain in the business. The law made radio a more lucrative venture, analysts said.

"Some of the speculation was whether radio could be a big enough business to be of interest to Disney," Nesbitt Burns analyst James Goss said. "They must have more of an interest in staying in the business."
Earlier Monday, Disney's ABC Radio announced an agreement to acquire WDRQ-FM in Detroit and WJZW-FM in Washington from Chancellor and Evergreen for $105 million in cash.

Evergreen and Chancellor are shedding some stations as part of their agreed merger, which is set to close in the third quarter. The stations to be sold to ABC are among the 10 the companies agreed to acquire from Viacom Inc.
Analysts said the acquisition also would allow ABC to seek a larger market share in two cities where it has lagged.

For example, ABC Radio holds a 12 percent market share in Detroit, a market now dominated by Chancellor Broadcasting Co with 36 percent and Westinghouse Electric Corp's CBS with a 32 percent market share.
"ABC Radio has been looking for ways to grow" in the Top 10 market, Morgan Stanley analyst Frank Bodenchak said. "This goes a way to gaining market share."
Bodenchak said ABC Radio was trailing in market share as its competitors aggressively pursued acquisitions.
"Disney really has been sitting on the sidelines," Bodenchak said.

There have been a flurry of acquisitions in the past year, since enactment of the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which allowed for greater station ownership. The new law permits companies to own as many as eight radio outlets in any single large market, up from four, and places no overall cap on total ownership nationwide.
"Clearly, potential exists where it didn't before," Goss said.
Still, even if Disney decides to get out of radio, the two acquisitions would boost an eventual sale price, Schroder Wertheim analyst David Londoner said.
ABC owns 11 AM radio stations in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, San Francisco, Detroit, Fort Worth-Dallas, Washington, Atlanta and Minneapolis-St. Paul. It owns 10 FM stations in those same markets.
((-- Lisa Marie Pane, New York newsdesk, 212 859-1713))
